Compared to MI300X, the MI355X slightly cuts CU count per XCD and disables more CUs for yields. The GPU is somewhat narrower but makes up much of the gap with higher clock speeds. Fewer, higher-clocked CUs are seen as easier to utilize.

On low-precision matrix math, B200 SMs have twice the per-clock throughput of a CDNA 4 CU across a range of 16-bit and 8-bit types. AMD relies on a bigger, higher-clocked GPU to keep an overall throughput lead, but the gap with Nvidia isn't nearly as big as in vector compute.

With vector and higher-precision data types, MI355X keeps a huge throughput lead over Blackwell thanks to higher core count and clocks, making the CDNA line look very good for HPC workloads. Vector performance is slightly lower than MI300X due to the reduced CU count.

MI355X offers 288 GB of HBM3E at 8 TB/s versus B200's 180 GB at 7.7 TB/s, which helps when competing models run out of VRAM. Compute-to-bandwidth is still lower: about 0.05 bytes per FP32 FLOP versus about 0.10 on Blackwell.

LDS grows to 160 KB with doubled read bandwidth, but a CDNA 4 CU still has less in-core storage than a Blackwell SM. A Blackwell SM can keep about 164 KB of shared memory plus 92 KB of L1, versus 160 KB LDS plus a 32 KB L1 on CDNA 4.

Commenter citing Wafer's Kimi K3 benchmark: 8×MI355X (TP8) got 118 tok/s decode per stream and 952 tok/s peak aggregate (119/GPU), versus B300 at 172, 1,568 and 196. "On every row the B300 beat the MI355X." The only win was cost per hour, based on one rental aggregator site.

Several users dispute the $2.50/GPU-hr MI355X price used in the comparison. One says "No one is easily getting the MI355X's at $2.5/hr." Another found $2.95/hr on gpus.io, notes TensorWave just says "Talk to sales," and says no provider has the AMD chip in abundance. Users also criticized the lack of TCO analysis.

The benchmark write-up described a workaround in its Kimi K3 serving setup: zero-pad the head count from 12 to 16, run the fast kernel, then extract the real 12 heads. Commenters questioned whether such optimizations kept output correct; a Wafer employee replied that the deployment passed OpenRouter's accuracy checks (tau/GPQA, tool calling, coherency).

Users criticized the MI355X vs B200 comparison as unfair. The model doesn't fit in a single B200 node, so the B200 setup paid a cross-node all-reduce over RoCE v2 (~195 Gb/s), with no mention of InfiniBand. They also said the eval was poorly defined and couldn't be replicated.
